analysis.one_liner: Counts lobbyist-bundled donations against the bundler and bans lobbyist fundraising while Congress is in session.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors in July 2014, referred to the Senate Rules Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have tightened campaign finance rules in three ways. Any money a registered lobbyist bundles (collects from many donors and passes to a candidate or party) would count against the lobbyist's own legal contribution limit, closing a loophole that lets one person direct far more money than they could legally give. The bill would also narrow the exemption that lets part-time lobbyists avoid registering, stretching the measurement window from three months to two years so occasional lobbying counts. Finally, senators, representatives, and their campaign committees would be barred from soliciting campaign money from registered lobbyists any time their chamber was in session.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who want to know how much influence one paid advocate can buy; candidates who cannot rely on lobbyist bundling networks; and grassroots donors whose contributions compete less against bundled corporate money.

how_it_helps.text: Bundled contributions forwarded by a registered lobbyist would count as both a contribution by the lobbyist and by each original contributor, capping how much one lobbyist can direct to a single candidate or party committee.

The bill widens the lobbyist registration net by stretching the exemption for people whose lobbying takes less than 20% of their time from a 3-month window to a 2-year window, so more paid influencers must disclose and register.

Candidates and sitting members of both chambers could not solicit campaign funds from registered lobbyists while their chamber is in session, reducing the practice of asking lobbyists for money within days of affecting their clients' business.

analysis.who_pays: Registered lobbyists and the bundling networks around leadership PACs and party committees, who would face lower effective contribution ceilings and a blackout on asking for money during most of the legislative calendar.

drawbacks.text: The solicitation ban has a large carve-out: it applies only while a chamber is 'in session,' and adjournments or recesses shorter than 10 calendar days still count as in session, so members could still legally ask lobbyists for money during longer breaks.

The registration change could pull people with incidental lobbying duties into disclosure requirements, and critics of contribution limits generally argue such caps push money toward less traceable channels like super PACs rather than reducing it.

By counting bundled money against the bundler's own limits, the bill would reduce a fundraising channel that leadership PACs and party committees use to support members, which defenders of those committees describe as a cost to party coordination.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure and bundling limits would give voters a clearer picture of lobbyist money in elections at little cost to the public; the main honest objection is that the solicitation ban leaves the biggest loophole open (long recesses), so the bill would curb some influence-buying while leaving the largest windows untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which took no further action on it before the 113th Congress ended, so it died in committee without a hearing, vote, or cosponsor.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet (D-CO) introduced the bill on July 31, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor; the bill ended with zero cosponsors.
The action record shows no further steps after the committee referral: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the 113th Congress ended January 3, 2015, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Registered lobbyists and campaign bundlers are better off: no lobbyist had to register under the wider 2-year test, no bundled contributions counted against anyone's limits, and members remained free to solicit them for money throughout the legislative calendar.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and did not attract any cosponsors to it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 31, 2014 and took no further action—no hearing or vote—before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan pattern: a single Democrat introduced it and no one else in either party acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would force more of them to register, cap the money they can bundle for candidates, and ban member solicitations during most of the session calendar. Defeated, their disclosure and bundling practices stayed unchanged.

industries.industry: Leadership PACs and national party committees
industries.note: These committees rely heavily on bundled contributions that would now count against the bundler's own contribution limit, cutting a major fundraising channel. The bill's death preserved that channel.

industries.industry: Professional campaign fundraisers and bundling networks
industries.note: Bundling by lobbyists would face hard caps, but non-lobbyist bundling would be untouched, so the bill's defeat changed little for most professional fundraisers.
